# OLLNOVA TECHNOLOGIES LTD. v. ECOBEE TECHNOLOGIES ULC (Fed. Cir. 2026)
**Court:** U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit

**Docket Number:** 25-1045

**Date Decided:** June 4, 2026

Justia Opinion Summary
At trial, a jury found that the defendant had infringed at least one of the asserted patents (without specifying which), determined that the claims of one patent were not limited to well-understood or routine technology, found another patent’s claims invalid, and awarded the plaintiff lump sum damages.
In the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, the defendant moved to dismiss based on patent ineligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101, but the court denied these motions for the patents at issue, except for one where factual disputes precluded summary judgment. The court also denied the defendant’s post-trial motions, including challenges to the verdict form, jury instructions related to patent eligibility, and motions to exclude expert testimony.
The plaintiff, in turn, appealed the district court’s limitation on prejudgment interest. The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit reviewed the case and determined that the district court’s verdict form, which combined all asserted patents into a single infringement question, violated the defendant’s right to a unanimous verdict. The appellate court vacated both the infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial on those issues.
The court also vacated and remanded the § 101 eligibility determination for one patent, requiring further proceedings under the Alice framework. However, the court affirmed the district court’s findings that the asserted claims of two other patents were not directed to abstract ideas and that substantial evidence supported the jury’s verdict of infringement on one patent. Remaining evidentiary and interest issues were dismissed as moot.

# Opinion Summary - Ollnova Technologies, Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
Recently the Federal Circuit issued its opinion in *Ollnova Technologies, Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC*, a patent case we have been following because it attracted an amicus brief. In this case, the patent owner, Ollnova, appeals a district court’s denial of requested prejudgment interest, and the accused infringer, Ecobee, cross-appeals the district court’s decisions on jury instructions and multiple issues including eligibility, infringement, damages, and marking.
In an opinion authored by Judge Chen and joined by Judges Cunningham and Stark, the panel affirmed-in-part, dismissed-in-part, vacated the judgment, and remanded the case. This is our summary of the opinion.
> The jury returned a verdict that (i) found ecobee infringed at least one of the Asserted Patents (but without identifying which patent or patents); (ii) found the ’495 patent’s asserted claims were not directed only to ‘well-understood, routine, and conventional’ technology; (iii) found the ’282 patent’s asserted claims were invalid; and (iv) awarded Ollnova lump sum damages of $11.5 million covering the life of the patents.
Judge Chen then summarized the panel’s holdings:

> For the reasons below, we vacate the infringement and damages judgments and remand for proceedings consistent with this opinion, including a new trial on infringement and damages. We vacate and remand for further proceedings under *Alice* step two of the 35 U.S.C. § 101 analysis as to the ’495 patent.

# Federal Circuit Vacates Ollnova’s $11.5M Damages Award Against ecobee, Orders New Trial on Infringement and Damages
06.16.26
Recently, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit issued a precedential decision in Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC, Nos. 2025-1045, -1046 (June 4, 2026), vacating the infringement and damages judgments in a smart-thermostat patent case and remanding for a new trial.

Ollnova sued ecobee in the Eastern District of Texas, alleging that ecobee’s smart thermostat products infringed four patents directed to wireless communications improvements in building automation systems. The patents address technical issues such as limited bandwidth, power consumption, and communications failures in wireless building automation networks. The jury found that ecobee infringed at least one asserted patent but did not identify which patent; found that ecobee had not proven the asserted claims of the ’495 patent involved only well-understood, routine, and conventional technology for purposes of Alice step two; found the asserted claims of the ’282 patent invalid; and awarded Ollnova a lump-sum royalty of $11.5 million. Both parties appealed.

The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded. The Court vacated the infringement judgment because the verdict form improperly combined all asserted patents into a single infringement question. The form asked whether ecobee infringed “ANY” asserted claim of the asserted patents, without requiring the jury to identify which patent was infringed. Applying Optis Cellular Technology, LLC v. Apple Inc., the Court held that this created an impermissible risk of a non-unanimous general verdict: different jurors could have found infringement of different patents while still answering “yes.” Because the damages award depended on the infringement verdict, the Court also vacated the $11.5 million award.

# Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC

## Holding

The Federal Circuit vacated the infringement and damages judgments because the verdict form used a single infringement question for all asserted patents, creating an impermissible risk of a non-unanimous verdict. It also vacated and remanded the '495 patent § 101 ruling for Alice step-two proceedings because the jury was not instructed on the abstract idea or that the abstract idea could not supply the inventive concept, while affirming § 101 eligibility at Alice step one for the '887 and '371 patents and affirming denial of JMOL of noninfringement for the '371 patent.

## Why It Matters

The decision reinforces that multi-patent infringement verdict forms need patent-by-patent liability questions and that any jury role in Alice step two must be framed by the abstract idea identified at step one.

# The Federal Circuit’s Ollnova Decision Sharpens the Rules for Patent Verdict Forms and § 101 Jury Instructions

# Ollnova v. ecobee: Federal Circuit Reaffirms the Requirements for Patent Jury Instructions and Verdict Forms

By: [Johnson Kuncheria](fenwick.com/people/johnson-kuncheria) , [Johnathan Chai](fenwick.com/people/johnathan-chai)

### What You Need To Know

* The Federal Circuit’s decision in _Ollnova v. ecobee_ reinforces its 2025 holding in _Optis_ on the requirements for patent verdict forms and 35 U.S.C. § 101 jury instructions.
* A patent verdict form must present infringement questions at least on a patent-by-patent basis; more detailed questions may be appropriate in some cases.
* If the jury will decide conventionality at _Alice_ Step Two, the court must instruct the jury as to the abstract idea at Step One and that the abstract idea itself cannot supply the inventive concept.

Recently in [_Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC_](cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/25-1045.OPINION.6-4-2026_2704652.pdf) , the Federal Circuit reaffirmed its prior decision in [_Optis Cellular Tech., LLC v. Apple Inc._](cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/22-1925.OPINION.6-16-2025_2530981.pdf) , 139 F.4th 1363 (Fed. Cir. 2025), requiring that (1) patent verdict forms present the infringement question at least on a patent-by-patent basis; and (2) the jury receive an instruction on the § 101 abstract idea when it is asked to determine whether an inventive concept exists. No. 2025-1045, 2026 WL 1596936, at \*8, \*11 (Fed. Cir. June 4, 2026).

Authored and Edited by Ryan V. McDonnell ; Erik R. Puknys ; *Renée Doser
In Ollnova Technologies Ltd., v. ecobee Technologies ULC, No. 2025-1045, 2025-1046 (Fed. Cir. June 4, 2026) , the Federal Circuit vacated and remanded an infringement and $11.5 million damages judgment, vacated and remanded the jury’s patent eligibility determination for the ’495 patent, and affirmed the district court’s determination that the claims of the ’887 and ’371 patents were not directed to abstract ideas at Alice step one.

...

The Federal Circuit first addressed the verdict forms. The court held that the district court abused its discretion by including on the verdict form a single infringement question covering all asserted patents because that did not ensure a unanimous verdict. It also determined that the jury instructions and verdict form related to patent eligibility for the ’495 patent were erroneous because they failed to identify that the claims were directed to an abstract idea and that this abstract idea could not supply the inventive concept. As a result, the court vacated and remanded for a new trial on infringement and damages for all patents and for further proceedings under Alice step two as to the ’495 patent.
On the merits, the Federal Circuit held that judgment as a matter of law of patent ineligibility for the ’495 patent was unwarranted because a reasonable jury could have found that the claimed dual-network architecture was not well-understood, routine, or conventional. The court also affirmed the district court’s determination that the claims of the ’887 and ’371 patents were not directed to an abstract idea because they claimed specific technological solutions to identified problems.

seltz.snippet:

In *Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC*, the Federal Circuit handed Ollnova a string of doctrinal wins — three of its four patents cleared the patent eligibility hurdle under 35 U.S.C. § 101 — only to throw out the entire $11.5 million verdict over a single defect in the verdict form. This decision serves a sharp reminder that in a multi-patent jury trial, how you ask the question can matter as much as the answer.

### **The Background**

Ollnova sued ecobee in the Eastern District of Texas (before Judge Rodney Gilstrap) on four patents covering wireless building automation systems (BAS)— U.S. Patent Nos. 7,860,495 (’495 patent), 8,264,371 (’371 patent), 7,746,887 (’887 patent), and 8,224,282 (’282 patent). The patents-in-suit address familiar challenges in wireless control networks: noisy channels, limited bandwidth, and the power drain that comes from devices constantly monitoring and broadcasting data. The asserted claims describe techniques for cutting down on unnecessary communications — transmitting only when a monitored value changes or crosses a threshold, and aggregating updates rather than streaming them continuously.

# The Federal Circuit’s Ollnova Decision Sharpens the Rules for Patent Verdict Forms and § 101 Jury Instructions
By: [Casey J. Lincoln](https://www.mofo.com/people/casey-lincoln)
How much precision do patent jury verdict forms require? And how should district courts instruct juries on the factual issues underlying Section 101 patent eligibility? In *Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC*, Nos. 2025-1045, -1046 (Fed. Cir. June 4, 2026), the Federal Circuit addressed both questions and, in doing so, vacated an infringement verdict and $11.5 million damages award.
Ollnova sued ecobee in the Eastern District of Texas, alleging that ecobee’s smart thermostats infringed four patents related to wireless communications in building automation systems. The case reached the jury with a partially resolved § 101 patent-eligibility issue as to one of the asserted patents. The district court had held that the ’495 patent was directed to an abstract idea under *Alice* step one, yet declined to resolve step two, finding that factual disputes remained as to whether the asserted limitations were “well-understood, routine, and conventional.”
The jury ultimately returned a verdict of infringement, resolved the ’495 patent’s step-two factual dispute in Ollnova’s favor, and awarded $11.5 million in lump-sum damages. But the trial structure left two problems. The infringement verdict form asked only whether ecobee infringed “ANY” asserted claim of “the Asserted Patents,” without requiring the jury to identify which patent was infringed. And the § 101 instructions did not tell the jury what abstract idea was identified by the district court at *Alice* step one or that the abstract idea itself could not supply the inventive concept at step two. Both of these issues, the Federal Circuit held, constitute reversible error.
**The Verdict Form:** The Federal Circuit first held that the district court abused its discretion by submitting a single combined infringement question.
